definition: Tirade means a long, angry speech full of harsh language.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word tirade. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know tirade should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One wrong turn set the GPS-hating cabbie off on a tirade that lasted from the bridge to my doorstep.
A complaint can be one calm sentence at the returns counter — the mildest ancestor of a tirade.
An outburst flares and is over; it stops short of a tirade, which sustains the anger for minutes on end.

A diatribe is a bitter, sustained attack that can be spoken or written — a review, a pamphlet, a speech. A tirade is always a voice: long, angry talk pouring out uninterrupted. Every tirade is heard; a diatribe may be read in silence.

A screed is a long, tedious complaint, usually written — the twelve-page letter to the editor nobody finishes. A tirade is delivered live and runs hot; a screed sits on the page and runs long. Boredom is the screed's signature, anger the tirade's.

A harangue is a lengthy, aggressive lecture aimed at its listeners — it wants to browbeat you into agreement. A tirade is purer anger: it vents rather than persuades, and needs no point beyond the fury itself. You escape a harangue unconvinced; you escape a tirade deafened.

A tirade is measured in minutes, not sentences: one voice, harsh language, no pauses for reply.
A flash of temper is an outburst; a tirade is an outburst that refuses to end — the anger has found its rhythm and means to keep it.
Tirade names the speech, not the speaker's act: long, angry, uninterrupted.
A brief flare is an outburst; a formal denunciation by vote is a censure (see this unit's reference list); and railing (this unit) is the activity — a tirade is often what it produces.

The night the health inspector left, Chef Almeida gathered the line cooks and delivered what the staff still calls the great walk-in tirade.
It lasted eleven minutes by the dishwasher's watch.
It began with the unlabeled containers, moved through the history of every shortcut he had ever witnessed, and ended, hoarse, somewhere near the subject of his own culinary school days.
No one was asked to do anything.
No list was posted afterward.
The speech demanded nothing; it simply poured out of him until it was gone.
The sous-chef, who had survived four of these, kept chopping shallots through all of it, nodding at intervals like a man waiting out weather.
By service the next evening, Almeida was humming at the pass, the storm spent, the kitchen spotless without a single order having been given.
